HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN)  -- Zimbabwe police arrested on Friday a magistrate who ordered the release of a senior opposition politician granted bail by the country's High Court, a lawyer said. A Zimbabwean policeman patrols outside the entrance of Mutare Magistrates court. The order to release the politician had been suspended when state lawyers appealed the HIgh Court decision. Trust Maanda, a lawyer in Mutare city about 300 kilometers (186 miles) east of Harare, told CNN by phone that magistrate Livingstone Chipadze had been arrested. "He is in police custody. The police are saying he ordered the release of Roy Bennett in compliance with the High Court ruling," said Maanda. Bennett is the choice of the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) for deputy agriculture minister under the power-sharing government formed last month. On Wednesday, Chipadze ordered Bennett be released from a prison in Mutare as had been ruled by the High Court last week. However, that order, which required Bennett to post $2,000 as bail, was suspended after the state filed an appeal with Zimbabwe's Supreme Court. "I can confirm the arrest, but I will be in position to tell you the charge he will face later," said a police official in Mutare over the phone. "He is likely to go to court on Saturday or Monday. But most magistrates here [in Mutare] have gone on strike over his arrest." Chipadze joins Bennett in prison in Mutare. Bennett was arrested on February 13 and is facing charges of possessing arms for the purposes of banditry, terrorism and sabotage. The continued detention of Bennett, an ally of MDC leader and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai, is seen by many as a crack in the foundation of the coalition Tsvangirai formed with President Robert Mugabe. Meanwhile, a Zimbabwe High Court judge Friday ordered the immediate release of three human rights activists in state "safe custody" to testify against human rights activist Jestina Mukoko, who is facing charges of plotting to topple Mugabe. Opposition MDC activists Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona have been missing since October last year after they were abducted from their homes under the cover of darkness. Lawyers Chris Mhike and Innocent Chagonda took the state to the High Court in an attempt to win the release the trio. But the state represented by Nelson Mutsonziwa had opposed the application, saying the three would be state witnesses when the trial of Mukoko starts. The MDC lawyers then successfully argued that the three were bread winners for their families and the state had not provided their families with assistance while they are in custody. Delivering the judgment, Justice Ben Hlatswayo said, "I order the immediate release of Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona from police custody or the custody of any other state agent. This order stands enforceable notwithstanding the noting or filing of an appeal." Relatives of the three who were milling around the High Court could not hide their joy after Mhike told them of Hlatswayo's ruling.

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) -- According to a lawyer, Zimbabwean police detained a magistrate on Friday who had directed that a top opposition figure—granted bail through the country's High Court—be freed.

Officers were seen standing guard at the entrance to the Mutare Magistrates court. The directive to free the politician had been put on hold after government attorneys challenged the High Court's ruling.

Speaking to CNN over the telephone, Trust Maanda—a lawyer based in Mutare, a city roughly 300 kilometers (186 miles) to the east of Harare—reported that authorities had taken magistrate Livingstone Chipadze into custody. "He is being held by police. According to them, he directed that Roy Bennett be freed in line with what the High Court had decided," Maanda explained.

The Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), the opposition party, has selected Bennett to serve as deputy agriculture minister within the power-sharing administration that was established the previous month. On Wednesday, following the High Court's decision from the prior week, Chipadze instructed that Bennett be freed from a Mutare prison. That instruction, which stipulated Bennett pay a $2,000 bail, was nonetheless put on hold once the government lodged a challenge with Zimbabwe's Supreme Court.

"I can verify that he has been arrested, though I'll only be able to share the specific charge against him at a later point," a Mutare police official stated during a phone conversation. "He'll probably appear in court either Saturday or Monday. However, the majority of magistrates in Mutare have stopped working in protest of his detention." Chipadze is now imprisoned in Mutare alongside Bennett.

Detained on February 13, Bennett stands accused of possessing weapons intended for use in banditry, terrorism, and sabotage. A close associate of Prime Minister and MDC leader Morgan Tsvangirai, Bennett's ongoing imprisonment is widely regarded as a fracture threatening the coalition that Tsvangirai established together with President Robert Mugabe.

Separately, a judge in Zimbabwe's High Court on Friday directed that three human rights campaigners being held in state "safe custody" be released without delay. These individuals were being detained so they could give evidence against fellow activist Jestina Mukoko, who has been charged with conspiring to overthrow Mugabe.

The three opposition MDC campaigners—Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa, and Terry Musona—had vanished since October of the previous year, having been seized from their residences during the night. Attorneys Chris Mhike and Innocent Chagonda brought the matter before the High Court in a bid to secure the men's freedom. However, the government, represented by Nelson Mutsonziwa, resisted the request, arguing that the three men were to serve as witnesses for the state once Mukoko's trial began. The MDC's legal team then made the successful case that the men were the primary earners for their households and that the government had failed to support their families throughout their detention.

In handing down his decision, Justice Ben Hlatswayo declared, "I order the immediate release of Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona from police custody or the custody of any other state agent. This order stands enforceable notwithstanding the noting or filing of an appeal." Family members of the three men, who had gathered near the High Court, were unable to contain their happiness once Mhike shared news of Hlatswayo's decision with them.

In a development that has intensified tensions within Zimbabwe's fragile coalition government, police arrested magistrate Livingstone Chipadze on Friday. His arrest came in direct response to his decision to order the release of opposition politician Roy Bennett, a ruling he had made in compliance with an earlier High Court decision.

Bennett is a prominent figure within the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), having been selected as the party's nominee for the position of deputy agriculture minister under the power-sharing arrangement. Despite his political standing, he faces serious criminal charges, including the possession of arms for the purposes of banditry, terrorism, and sabotage—accusations that have become a focal point of contention between the country's rival political factions.

The legal situation grew more complicated when the magistrate's order to release Bennett on $2,000 bail was suspended. State lawyers moved swiftly to file an appeal with Zimbabwe's Supreme Court, effectively blocking Bennett's release and keeping him in custody pending further legal proceedings.

Chipadze's arrest has provoked a strong reaction from the legal community in Mutare, where most magistrates have gone on strike in protest. Their demonstration underscores concerns about judicial independence and the treatment of court officials who issue rulings unfavorable to the state. Adding to the irony of the situation, Chipadze now finds himself imprisoned alongside Bennett, the very man whose release he had ordered.

Beyond the immediate legal drama, Bennett's continued detention carries significant political weight. It is widely viewed as a crack in the foundation of the coalition government formed between Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai and President Robert Mugabe. The episode highlights the deep mistrust and unresolved power struggles that continue to threaten the stability of Zimbabwe's power-sharing agreement.

# The Arrest of Magistrate Livingstone Chipadze

In a move that sent shockwaves through Zimbabwe's judicial system, police arrested magistrate Livingstone Chipadze after he ordered the release of prominent opposition politician Roy Bennett. The magistrate had acted in compliance with a High Court ruling that called for Bennett's release, believing he was upholding the rule of law. However, the situation was complicated by the fact that the release order had already been suspended following an appeal by the state to the Supreme Court. This procedural conflict placed Chipadze in an untenable position, caught between competing legal directives.

## Judicial Protest and Solidarity

The arrest of one of their own galvanized the legal community in Mutare, where most magistrates responded by going on strike in protest. Their walkout represented a rare and pointed demonstration of judicial solidarity, signaling deep concern over what many viewed as intimidation of the judiciary and interference with the independence of the courts. By downing their gavels, the magistrates sent an unmistakable message that the arrest of a colleague for carrying out his judicial duties threatened the integrity of the entire legal system.

## Implications for the Power-Sharing Government

Beyond its immediate impact on the courts, the incident was widely interpreted as placing significant strain on Zimbabwe's fragile power-sharing arrangement. This delicate political settlement had brought together Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) leader Morgan Tsvangirai and long-serving President Robert Mugabe in an uneasy coalition. Roy Bennett's case was especially sensitive because of his prominent position within the opposition—he had been nominated to serve as the MDC's deputy agriculture minister. His continued detention, and now the arrest of the magistrate who sought his release, underscored the persistent tensions and mutual distrust between the two political camps.

The episode highlighted the fundamental challenges facing the unity government, raising questions about whether genuine cooperation was possible when the machinery of the state could still be used against opposition figures and those who sought to protect their legal rights.

**HARARE, Zimbabwe** — A Zimbabwean magistrate who granted bail to prominent opposition politician Roy Bennett was briefly detained by authorities, in a move that opposition officials and human rights groups condemned as an assault on the country's fragile judicial independence.

The magistrate had ruled that Bennett, a senior official in the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), should be released on bail after weeks in custody on charges his party described as politically motivated. Shortly after the ruling, the magistrate was taken into custody by state security agents, according to opposition sources and legal observers.

Bennett, a former farmer and treasurer-general of the MDC, was arrested earlier on allegations related to terrorism, banditry and insurgency — charges his lawyers and supporters have dismissed as fabricated. His detention came at a politically sensitive moment, as the MDC prepared to join a power-sharing government with President Robert Mugabe's ZANU-PF party.

"This is a clear attempt to intimidate the judiciary and undermine the rule of law," an MDC spokesman said. "The magistrate simply applied the law, and for that he has been targeted."

Human rights organizations expressed alarm at the reported detention, warning that the harassment of judicial officers threatened confidence in Zimbabwe's courts. "When judges and magistrates cannot make rulings without fear of arrest, the entire justice system is compromised," said a representative of a Harare-based legal rights group.

The incident deepened concerns about the durability of Zimbabwe's unity government, formed after disputed elections and months of negotiations mediated by regional leaders. Bennett's case became a flashpoint, with the MDC insisting on his release as a test of the new administration's commitment to reform.

State officials did not immediately comment on the magistrate's detention or provide details of any charges. Government representatives have previously maintained that the cases against opposition figures are being handled according to the law.

Bennett has long been a controversial figure in Zimbabwean politics. A vocal critic of Mugabe's government, he previously served a prison term after a physical altercation in parliament and spent time in exile in neighboring South Africa before returning to the country.

The MDC called for Bennett's immediate and unconditional release and demanded assurances that judicial officials would be protected from political interference.

*This is a developing story.*

---

*Note: This article is based on real events surrounding Roy Bennett's 2009 detention. Some details have been generalized, and readers seeking precise information should consult contemporaneous news reports.*

counterfactuals.output:
HARARE, Zimbabwe — The fragile power-sharing government that Zimbabwe's rival political parties assembled with such difficulty a year ago is straining once again over the continued legal ordeal of Roy Bennett, the opposition figure whose case has become a lightning rod for the deep mistrust dividing the coalition.

Bennett, a former coffee farmer and treasurer-general of Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai's Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), remains in legal limbo. Designated as deputy minister of agriculture under the terms of the September 2008 power-sharing agreement, he has never been sworn into office. President Robert Mugabe has refused to formally appoint him, citing the terrorism and weapons charges that have shadowed Bennett for the better part of a year.

"This is not simply about one man," a senior MDC official said in an interview here, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the negotiations. "It is about whether the other side intends to honor anything it signed. If they can hold Roy hostage, they can hold the whole agreement hostage."

The charges against Bennett stem from allegations that he plotted acts of banditry, sabotage and terrorism aimed at unseating Mr. Mugabe's government — accusations his lawyers describe as politically manufactured. He was arrested at Charles Prince Airport in February of last year, on the very day that Mr. Tsvangirai was sworn in as prime minister, a coincidence of timing that opposition supporters have long cited as evidence of a calculated humiliation.

Prosecutors have leaned heavily on the testimony of Peter Hitschmann, an arms dealer whose earlier statements implicating Bennett were later recanted in court, where Hitschmann testified that they had been extracted under duress and torture. Defense attorneys have argued repeatedly that the state's case has effectively collapsed, and Bennett was eventually released on bail after months in detention, only to remain barred from taking up his ministerial post.

The impasse has exposed the structural weakness at the heart of the Global Political Agreement, the accord brokered under the auspices of the Southern African Development Community. That deal divided ministries and authority between ZANU-PF and the two MDC formations, but left crucial questions of appointment and enforcement subject to the good faith of parties who trust one another very little.

For ZANU-PF, the Bennett case is a matter of law, not politics. "No one is above the courts," a spokesman for the party said, insisting that Mr. Mugabe was entitled to withhold an appointment while criminal proceedings were pending. Officials aligned with the president have also raised Bennett's history as a bitter symbol of the country's contested land reforms; his farm in the eastern highlands was among thousands seized during the often-violent redistribution program of the past decade.

Western diplomats stationed in the capital say the standoff is being watched closely as a barometer of whether the coalition can deliver the reforms that donors have demanded before releasing significant reconstruction aid to an economy only beginning to stabilize after years of hyperinflation. The introduction of the U.S. dollar and the South African rand as functioning currencies has ended the era of trillion-dollar banknotes, and shops in Harare are stocked again, but political conditions attached to broader assistance remain unmet.

Inside the Cabinet, the friction has spilled into other disputes — over the composition of the central bank, the attorney general's office and the provincial governorships — all of them contested appointments that the MDC says Mr. Mugabe has filled unilaterally in violation of the agreement. Mr. Tsvangirai briefly disengaged from the government last year in protest, a walkout that underscored how close the arrangement has come to collapse.

Bennett himself has kept a comparatively low public profile, appearing at court dates and consulting with his legal team while declining to inflame the situation with rhetoric. Supporters gathered outside the High Court during recent hearings, some carrying placards, others simply watching in silence as he arrived. His lawyers have signaled they will press for a definitive dismissal of the charges, arguing that continued prosecution amounts to an abuse of process.

Regional mediators have urged patience, and SADC leaders have periodically summoned the principals to summits in Pretoria and elsewhere to shore up the deal. But analysts here caution that the goodwill required to resolve the Bennett matter appears to be in short supply.

"The agreement was designed to force enemies to govern together," said a Harare-based political analyst. "What it did not do was give either side a reason to concede on the cases that matter most to them personally. Bennett is exactly such a case."

For now, the deputy minister-designate waits — neither fully free nor fully in office — his status a daily reminder of how much of Zimbabwe's political future remains unsettled, and how little the men who signed the power-sharing accord have managed to agree upon since.

Zimbabwe's judicial system found itself at the center of national attention this week as two significant legal matters unfolded—one involving the arrest of a serving magistrate, and another concerning the fate of three opposition activists whose case had drawn accusations of enforced disappearance.

In a development that raised questions about judicial independence and the treatment of court officials, magistrate Livingstone Chipadze was taken into custody by authorities. The arrest of a sitting magistrate is an unusual occurrence that has drawn scrutiny from legal observers and civil society organizations, who have called for transparency regarding the circumstances and charges involved.

Legal analysts noted that the detention of judicial officers carries particular sensitivity in Zimbabwe, where concerns about the separation of powers and pressure on the courts have periodically surfaced. Observers emphasized the importance of due process being followed and of the magistrate's own rights being protected under the law.

## High Court Orders Release of Three MDC Activists

In a separate but equally significant ruling, the High Court ordered the release of three activists affiliated with the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), following reports that they had been abducted.

The case had generated alarm among human rights groups, who characterized the disappearance of the activists as part of a troubling pattern of alleged enforced disappearances targeting opposition figures and government critics. The High Court's intervention was welcomed by the activists' legal representatives and supporters, who had petitioned the court for their safe return.

The ruling underscored the role of the judiciary as a potential check on extrajudicial actions, even as broader questions persisted about accountability for those responsible for the alleged abductions.

## Broader Context

Both cases arrive against a backdrop of longstanding concerns—raised by domestic and international rights organizations—regarding the state of civil liberties, judicial independence, and political freedoms in Zimbabwe. The MDC and other opposition groups have frequently alleged harassment of their members, while government officials have often disputed such characterizations.

Human rights advocates have called for thorough investigations into the circumstances of the activists' abduction and for the perpetrators to be held accountable. Simultaneously, legal professionals have urged that the case involving magistrate Chipadze be handled with strict adherence to legal procedure.

As these cases proceed, they are likely to remain focal points in ongoing debates over governance, accountability, and the rule of law in Zimbabwe.

# Opposition Tensions Mount as Zimbabwe's Unity Government Faces New Strains

**HARARE** — Political tensions escalated in Zimbabwe this week as opposition figures within the country's fragile power-sharing government faced renewed legal challenges, raising questions about the durability of the coalition between President Robert Mugabe and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai.

Several senior members of Tsvangirai's Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) reported harassment by state security forces, according to party officials, who characterized the actions as attempts to undermine the opposition's role in the unity government formed following disputed elections.

The power-sharing arrangement, brokered through regional mediation, had been intended to stabilize a nation battered by economic collapse and political violence. However, persistent disputes over key appointments and the treatment of opposition members have exposed deep fissures within the administration.

"These continued arrests and intimidation tactics violate both the letter and spirit of our agreement," an MDC spokesperson said, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of ongoing negotiations. "We cannot govern effectively while our members face persecution."

Officials aligned with Mugabe's ZANU-PF party dismissed the accusations, insisting that legal proceedings against certain individuals reflected legitimate law enforcement rather than political targeting. State media has portrayed the detentions as routine matters unrelated to the opposition's standing in government.

Human rights organizations operating in the region expressed concern over the developments. Observers noted that the treatment of opposition figures would serve as a critical test of Mugabe's commitment to genuine power-sharing.

The friction comes amid broader disputes over control of key ministries, particularly those governing security and finance. Analysts suggest these portfolios represent the true battleground for influence within the coalition.

"The unity government exists more on paper than in practice," said a regional political analyst based in Johannesburg. "Without resolution on these fundamental issues, the coalition risks collapse."

Tsvangirai, who endured years of persecution before entering government, has faced criticism from some supporters who question whether meaningful reform remains possible within the current framework. The prime minister has repeatedly called for full implementation of agreed reforms.

International donors have signaled that continued financial assistance depends on demonstrable progress toward political stability and rule of law. Western governments have maintained targeted measures against certain officials, contributing to ongoing diplomatic complexities.

As the standoff continues, ordinary Zimbabweans remain caught between competing political forces, awaiting evidence that their leaders can bridge divisions and address the nation's pressing economic challenges.

*(Additional reporting from regional bureaus)*
